THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 7

MANNERS AND CUSTOMS.—Equally enlightening and interesting is Mr. Carter's observation of some points of manners and customs of a people who were becoming homogeneous in their development of the section:

Native peculiarities and cosmopolitan ideas have combined to produce some strange manners and customs among the people of this county.

This peculiarity is naturally noticed in all classes. As a general thing, among lawyers for instance, a man will be consulted frankly on the merits of the society of which he is a member; but not so here. A lawyer or a doctor is an exception, and the general public is quite free to make such statement. The members of fractional class have none of the bland suave manners, peculiar to the doctor. No, they are apt to be a little rough.

The people seem to think that the professional man was made for the officers of their own class. His confidence was made for all the citizens of the rural community, not offered to any objector.

In every kind of labor, except perhaps on farms, the ten-hour system seems to prevail over all here. Men not accustomed to it, the men, during the season not accustomed to it, look, upon it something of a wonder. The sun is high in the heavens.

During a certain week in each month, the public square is a scene of busy life, and the streets around it are crowded with people. This is the day for the sale or stray stock, and since the establishment of the town on the "first Monday" to buy critics, the people have grazed from far and near, and the show of stock reaches grand proportions. Every man on the square is a trader, and trading is the principal occupation; a good time, and every man thinks he lives in the best country, if the sun is in the day's possession.
